title: Prefetch predictor & eviction heuristic exploratory notes
content:
Purpose:
Quick exploratory notes on a low-cost predictor + prefetch policy and complementary eviction tweaks. Goal is to reduce tail latency and memory bandwidth peaks for chat workloads with highly skewed KV reuse while keeping remote spill/paging within acceptable bounds. This is intentionally rough — experiments done on rtx-cluster-4 and staging traces (jan-2025)

Background/context:
- We see repeated expensive page faults and DRAM bursts for long-context chat where KV pages are scattered across physical memory channels.
- Existing LRU-ish eviction with time-based warmup handles steady-state OK but suffers under sudden prefix churn (e.g., multi-turn assistant sessions that jump topics).
- Previous notes focused on eviction thresholds and sampling windows; this explores adding a tiny predictor that drives selective prefetch + soft-reservations to smooth bandwidth.

Hypotheses:
1) A short-term reuse predictor (window=8 requests, feature: token overlap + last-seen delta) can identify ~60–70% of soon-to-be-reused KV entries with <5% false positives. Prefetching those reduces average latency by ~5–12ms for 99th percentile.
2) Combined with conservative soft-reservations (pin top-2 predicted pages per session for 200ms), it reduces page-in spikes and evictions churn, lowering memory bandwidth variance by ~20%.
3) Incorrect prefetches increase read amplification and could hurt throughput if predictor precision <55%; we need fallback to disable for high-throughput bursts.

Microbench setup:
- Workload: synthetic chat traces (scale factor 5×), and 10k sampled production sessions (anonymized) from 2025-01.
- Nodes: rtx-cluster-4, 8x A100-like GPUs but CPU & memory behavior isolated (we run only single-suite tests).
- Baseline: current kv-evict=adaptive-ttl (default params), prefetch disabled.
- New experiment: predictor_v1 + prefetch async (nonblocking IO) + soft-reserve (200ms TTL).
- Metrics captured: per-request latency (p50/p95/p99), pagefault/sec, DRAM bandwidth instantaneous (sampled 10ms), KV hit/reuse rates, eviction churn (pages evicted/sec), cpu overhead from predictor.

Predictor details (v1):
- Features to compute per-request: last_seen_delta (ms), token_prefix_hash64 (simple rolling), session_reuse_count (last 60s), request_seq_delta (position delta in conversation).
- Simple scoring: score = w1*(last_seen_delta < 500ms) + w2*(prefix_hash_match) + w3*(reuse_count>1). We tuned w's via grid search on small trace.
- Threshold chosen for target precision ~62%.

Preliminary results (aggregate):
- Predictor precision: 61.8%, recall: 66.3% (on sampled validation trace).
- p99 latency: baseline 183ms -> predictor+prefetch 170ms (7% improvement). p95: 84ms -> 78ms. p50 unchanged within noise.
- Pagefault/sec: baseline mean 12.4 -> 9.1 (-26%).
- DRAM bandwidth 95th percentile: baseline 124 GB/s -> 101 GB/s (-18%). Instantaneous variance (stddev) reduced ~22%.
- Eviction churn: evictions/sec baseline 210 -> 178 (-15%).
- CPU overhead: predictor compute ~0.6% of request CPU time; async prefetch IO threads added 4% peak CPU for IO.
- False-positive cost: extra read amplification approximated +3% tokens served from memory reads, but overall cost saved via fewer page-ins.

Profiling notes (how we measured):
- Used perf counters on host + nvml telemetry for GPU local DRAM. For memory channels we used Linux perf mem traces and Intel pcm-dram (where available).
- Timestamps aligned with request ids; page-in events correlated with request boundary to estimate causal prefetch benefit.
- Observed hotspots: prefetch threads occasionally contend on IO queue when predictor triggers >8 prefetches at once for a single burst; mitigated by queue-depth cap and per-session rate limit.

Failure modes observed:
- High-throughput bursts (rush tests) where many short sessions start simultaneously: predictor precision drops to ~48% because short sessions don't build enough history -> prefetching causes IO storms that slightly increase 99th latency. We added a simple throughput-aware inhibit (disable predictor when outstanding-requests > 2k).
- Long-tail cold sessions: predictor not useful; should fallback to current adaptive policies (no prefetch).
- Edge-case: when model requests jump between distant context windows (prefix_hash collisions), predictor may mislead — adding a second-check using approximate locality (page neighbourhood) reduced bad prefetch by 6%.

Design options considered:
A) Keep predictor simple (current) and only prefetch top-1 per session. Minimal overhead, small wins.
B) More sophisticated model (lightweight RNN or Bloom filter over last-64 keys) — higher recall but CPU + memory cost; needs careful cost-benefit.
C) Opportunistic cooperative eviction: when predictor pins pages, mark other low-score pages with higher eviction priority to make room proactively. Risk: harming other sessions' latency.
D) Bandwidth-aware throttling: adapt prefetch rate to instantaneous DRAM bandwidth headroom (feedback loop). Promising to avoid IO spikes.

Action items (next steps):
- A1: Run longer 24h job on real production sampling with predictor-v1 + bandwidth-aware throttle enabled. Capture cost delta (token-level) and downstream request error rates. Assignee: Marco. Due: 2025-02-25.
- A2: Implement inhibit rule for high outstanding load in runtime (simple k/v). Assignee: Sofia. Due: 2025-02-16 (in flight).
- A3: Prototype small Bloom-approx predictor (offline) to measure recall/precision trade. Assignee: Ben. Due: 2025-03-03.
- A4: Add telemetry events for prefetch decisions (why prefetched, score, outcome) to help future model training. Assignee: Aisha. Due: 2025-02-20.

Open questions / risks:
- What is acceptable extra I/O read amplification before economics flip negative? Need finance to model token vs bandwidth costs across hosted vs dedicated customers.
- How to make policy transparent to Console (observability)? We need to show prefetch hits, disabled-by-inhibit, and candidate pages.
- Safety: ensure predictor cannot be gamed by adversarial prompts that force huge prefetch budgets. Add per-session caps.

Notes to self / rough TODOs:
- Add small unit test harness that can inject synthetic reuse patterns (zipfian vs uniform) and measure predictor behavior deterministically.
- Post-mortem metrics to add: per-session prefetch ROI (latency saved vs extra IO).
- Consider merging with existing adaptive-ttl as mode: predictor-on-demand mode toggled per model or customer tier.

References / links:
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/482 (prefetch async plumbing)
- Jira: JIRA-ENG-3421 (kv-prefetch experiment tracking)
- Confluence draft: confluence.company/kv-prefetch-design (internal)

End log.
summary: Exploratory notes for a lightweight KV reuse predictor + selective prefetch policy that reduced p99 latency and DRAM bandwidth spikes in early tests; includes hypotheses, microbench results, failure modes, and next steps.
